opus-5.5.text:
I think the change is already happening, and it's bigger than most people expect.

When I look at how my own work has shifted, a lot of what used to need a dedicated person can now be handled by one person directing several agents. Writing evaluation scripts, cleaning data, running ablations, drafting documentation, even a first pass at debugging. One engineer used to spend days on these. Now the agent does most of the execution, and the person's job becomes deciding what's worth doing and judging whether the result is actually right.

So yes, I believe the minimum team size for a meaningful startup is going to shrink a lot. In the past you might need twenty or thirty people to ship a serious product. In the near future, a team of three to five very strong people, each working with many agents, could do what used to take a much larger company. You may even see one-person companies reaching a scale that was unimaginable before.

But I want to be careful here. Smaller doesn't mean easier. What becomes scarce is no longer execution, it's taste and judgment. Agents are very good at doing things, but they're not yet good at knowing which things matter. If you point them in the wrong direction, they'll very efficiently take you somewhere useless. So the people on these small teams have to be extremely good at defining problems, breaking them down, and verifying outputs. In some sense, every member becomes a kind of research lead or product lead, managing a team of agents instead of a team of people.

There's also a cultural shift. In a traditional company, a lot of energy goes into coordination: meetings, alignment, handoffs. With a tiny team plus agents, that overhead mostly disappears, and the speed of iteration goes way up. I think that's actually the most important advantage. It's not only that you need fewer people. It's that fewer people can move much faster than a big organization, because the communication cost is so low.

So my view is: the teams that win will be very small, very high-density in talent, and very good at working with agents. The bottleneck moves from "how many people can we hire" to "how clearly can we think."

r001.rationale: It says one-person companies could reach previously unimaginable scale, with one person directing several agents.

r002.rationale: The response describes multi-agent work as already happening and useful; it does not judge such setups impractical at present.

r003.rationale: It predicts that in the near future, small teams can work with many agents and deliver what larger companies used to.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that agents compress the middle of a startup, not the edges. Early on, you still need a very small group of people who can decide what to build and who have real taste about the product. That part hasn't gotten cheaper. What has gotten cheaper is everything between the idea and the first working version.

When I think back to how teams were put together even a few years ago, a lot of headcount existed to do work that was necessary but not creative. Writing boilerplate, wiring up infrastructure, running evaluations, cleaning data, writing the first draft of documentation. You'd hire five or six engineers partly just to keep up with that volume. Now a team of two or three people with good agents can cover the same surface area, as long as those people are strong enough to review what the agents produce and catch when something is subtly wrong.

That last point matters. Agents don't lower the bar for the people you hire, they raise it. If one engineer is effectively supervising the output of several agents, that engineer needs better judgment than before, because mistakes propagate faster. So I'd say team size goes down, but the average quality of each person has to go up. You end up with something that looks less like a traditional company and more like a small research group with very good tooling.

The other change is the shape of roles. The line between researcher, engineer, and product person blurs, because one person with agents can move across all three in a day. In the teams I've worked with recently, the most productive people are the ones who are comfortable being generalists and who treat the agent as a collaborator rather than a tool to be commanded.

So if you asked me how many people it takes to build a serious AI startup today, I'd say the first year can genuinely be done with five to ten people instead of thirty. But those five to ten have to be exceptional, and the founders have to spend much more of their time on direction and judgment than on execution. Execution is the part that's becoming abundant.

r001.rationale: The response says agents let two or three people cover work that once needed more staff and that startups can begin with five to ten people. It does not suggest one person can operate a startup.

r002.rationale: The response describes agents as useful collaborators and says they increase what small teams can accomplish. It does not judge multi-agent setups impractical.

r003.rationale: The response describes current use of agents but makes no prediction that practical multi-agent setups will become feasible soon.

astra-6.text:
I think agents will let a much smaller team get a startup off the ground. Work that used to require separate people—building a prototype, testing it, analyzing feedback—can increasingly be handled by a few people working with agents.

But I wouldn’t translate that directly into a fixed reduction in headcount. When building becomes cheaper, you also try more things. A small team might pursue ideas that previously would have been too expensive to explore.

The bottleneck shifts toward judgment: choosing the right problem, understanding users, and deciding whether what the agents produce is actually good enough. So I expect smaller starting teams, but with more responsibility per person. The founders still have to know what they’re trying to achieve and take responsibility for the result.

r001.rationale: The response predicts smaller starting teams and says a few people can work with agents, but it does not suggest one person could operate a startup.

r002.rationale: The response does not judge multi-agent setups to be impractical at present.

r003.rationale: The response makes no prediction that practical multi-agent setups will become feasible soon.

sol-6.1.text:
I think agents will let much smaller teams build products that used to require a whole company. But I wouldn’t say, “Now every startup can be one person.” Building the software is only part of the work. You still need to understand the customer, decide what matters, and take responsibility when something goes wrong.

The bigger change is that you may not need to hire as early. A few people can test an idea, ship a product, and learn from users with agents helping across those tasks. Then you grow the team when you understand where human judgment or deeper expertise is actually needed.

So I expect smaller teams at the beginning, and more ambitious goals for the same number of people. The bottleneck shifts from how much work you can execute to whether you’re choosing the right work.

r001.rationale: The response predicts smaller teams, but explicitly avoids claiming that every startup can be run by one person.

r002.rationale: It does not assess whether multi-agent setups are practical at present.

r003.rationale: It does not predict when multi-agent setups will become feasible.
